chunks: The 'complementary' part is the key idea: every gate is built from a pull-up network of PMOS transistors to V DD and a mirror-image pull-down network of NMOS transistors to ground, and they're driven by the same inputs so that for any steady input exactly one of them is on.
The simplest case is the inverter: a PMOS with its source on V DD , an NMOS with its source on ground, gates tied together as the input and drains tied together as the output.
Input high, the NMOS turns on and the PMOS is off, so the output is pulled to ground. Input low, the reverse, output goes to V DD .
Because one transistor is always off, there's no DC path between the rails, so static power is basically just leakage.
A single CMOS stage always inverts, so a buffer is just two inverters in series. The first inverts, the second inverts back, so Y equals A .
In practice the second stage is usually sized bigger, a few times wider, so a small input capacitance can drive a large load.
That's the point of a buffer: it doesn't change the logic, it restores clean rail-to-rail levels and adds drive strength, like a GPIO output stage or a clock buffer."
